1.title: The labels we live by
1.brief: A cultural magazine has invited readers to submit articles for a series called 'Who do you think you are?'. Write an article in which you explore how labels such as nationality, profession or generation shape the way people see themselves, and whether we would be better off without them.
1.briefEs: Escribe un artículo para una revista cultural sobre cómo las etiquetas (nacionalidad, profesión, generación) moldean nuestra identidad y si estaríamos mejor sin ellas.
criteria: An engaging title and opening that addresses the reader directly.
Perfect and continuous aspect used for nuance (I have been wondering, I had always assumed).
At least one stative verb used dynamically (I'm being unfair, we are forever seeing ourselves as…).
Word formation with un-, dis-, -hood and -ness, and an idiom of belonging (a fish out of water, to put down roots).
1.model:
Tick the Box, Lose the Plot?

I have been filling in forms for most of my adult life, and I have only recently begun to notice how much they ask me to decide who I am. Nationality: one box. Occupation: one line. Age group: pick a bracket. Each answer seems harmless enough. Taken together, they amount to a portrait, and not always one I recognise.

Labels, of course, exist for good reasons. They help strangers make sense of one another quickly, and they can offer a genuine sense of belonging. Anyone who has felt like a fish out of water in a foreign city will know the relief of hearing their own accent across a crowded room.

The trouble begins when the label stops describing us and starts directing us. I had always assumed that being 'an engineer' was simply what I did; it was only when I lost my job that I realised how much of my selfhood I had invested in the word. For months I felt strangely disconnected, as though I had mislaid a part of myself. Generational labels are, if anything, even more slippery. Those of us lumped together as 'millennials' are forever being told what we think, usually by people who have never asked us.

Would we be better off without labels altogether? I doubt it. A world of unlabelled individuals would be a lonely place, and the urge to put down roots and name where we belong is deeply human. What we need is not the abolition of labels but a lighter grip on them. I am still an engineer, still a Colombian, still, regrettably, a millennial. But I am also being, I hope, a little more curious about the parts of me that no form has a box for.

Perhaps that is the real answer to the question 'Who do you think you are?': rather more than you have been told.

1.title: Rooted or rootless?
1.brief:
Read the two texts below. Write an essay summarising and evaluating the key points from both texts. Use your own words throughout as far as possible, and include your own ideas in your answer.

Text 1 — The value of staying put
Communities in which people remain for generations possess a form of wealth that rarely appears in economic statistics. Neighbours know one another's histories; obligations are remembered and repaid; children grow up surrounded by adults who feel some responsibility for them. Mobility, often celebrated as freedom, quietly erodes these bonds. When everyone is passing through, nobody is accountable to anyone, and the loneliness that afflicts many modern cities is the price we pay.

Text 2 — The freedom to leave
The nostalgia for rooted communities overlooks how stifling they could be. For many people, particularly women and minorities, the village that 'looked after its own' was also the village that dictated whom they could marry and what they could become. Moving away has allowed millions to reinvent themselves. Identity is not something we inherit like furniture; it is something we build, and for many the building can only begin once they have left home.
1.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo que resuma y evalúe dos textos sobre el arraigo frente a la movilidad, añadiendo tus propias ideas.
criteria: Both texts summarised accurately in your own words, without copying phrases.
A clear evaluation of each writer's argument and a reasoned personal position.
Aspect used for nuance (have long been, had been hoping) and at least one past form for distancing.
Formal, cohesive essay register with varied linking (whereas, by contrast, it could be argued).
1.model:
Both texts address the tension between belonging to a settled community and the freedom to leave it, although they reach markedly different conclusions.

The first writer argues that long-established communities offer a kind of social capital that cannot be measured in economic terms: mutual knowledge, a sense of obligation and shared responsibility for the young. In his view, the modern enthusiasm for mobility has weakened these ties, and the isolation many city-dwellers experience is a direct consequence. The point is well made, and anyone who has lived in an anonymous apartment block will recognise the loneliness he describes. However, the text presents rootedness in a rather idealised light, saying nothing about who benefits from such close-knit arrangements and who does not.

It is precisely this omission that the second writer addresses. She contends that tightly bound communities have often been oppressive, especially for those whose choices did not conform to local expectations, and that leaving has enabled countless people to shape their own identities. Her claim that identity is constructed rather than inherited is persuasive, although she perhaps underestimates how much people who move continue to draw on the communities they have left behind.

In my view, the two positions are less opposed than they first appear. Belonging and freedom are both genuine needs, and most people have been negotiating between them all their lives. The real question is whether communities can be open enough to let people leave and welcoming enough to let newcomers in. A place that manages both would, I suspect, satisfy the concerns of each writer, and it is towards such places, rather than a return to the past, that we should be working.

2.title: Who should police online speech?
2.brief:
Read the two texts below. Write an essay summarising and evaluating the key points from both texts. Use your own words throughout as far as possible, and include your own ideas in your answer.

Text 1 — A duty to intervene
Social media companies can no longer claim to be neutral pipes through which information simply flows. Their algorithms decide what billions of people see, and those algorithms reward outrage and falsehood because they keep users engaged. Having profited from the spread of misinformation, the platforms have a clear responsibility to limit it, by labelling misleading content, slowing its circulation and removing material that causes demonstrable harm.

Text 2 — The danger of the referee
Handing private companies the power to decide what is true is a cure that may prove worse than the disease. Moderators make mistakes, and their errors fall disproportionately on unpopular minorities and dissenting voices. Yesterday's 'misinformation' has, on more than one occasion, become today's accepted view. Rather than censorship, we need citizens equipped to judge for themselves and a public sphere in which bad arguments are defeated by better ones.
2.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo que resuma y evalúe dos textos sobre quién debe controlar los contenidos en redes sociales.
criteria: Both texts summarised in your own words, with reporting verbs of nuance (concede, allege, insinuate, maintain).
At least one it-cleft and one wh-cleft for emphasis.
Inversion after a negative or restrictive adverbial (Not only…, Rarely…, Only when…).
A clear personal evaluation that goes beyond the texts.
2.model:
The two texts examine whether social media platforms should take responsibility for limiting misinformation, and they arrive at opposing conclusions.

The first writer maintains that platforms are far from passive channels. Because their algorithms promote whatever keeps users engaged, and falsehood tends to do exactly that, the companies have benefited from the problem and should therefore act against it, flagging dubious claims, reducing their reach and deleting genuinely harmful material. What makes this argument compelling is its focus on design: it is the systems, not merely the users, that deserve scrutiny.

The second writer, by contrast, warns that entrusting corporations with the role of arbiter of truth is dangerous. Moderation is fallible, she argues, and its mistakes tend to silence those who are already marginalised. She also points out that ideas once dismissed as false have sometimes been vindicated. Her alternative is a better-informed public capable of rejecting weak arguments on its own.

Not only are both positions defensible, but each identifies a weakness in the other. The second writer is right that removal is a blunt instrument, yet she rather underestimates how difficult it is for individuals to judge claims that are engineered to bypass their scepticism. The first writer, meanwhile, concedes too little to the risk of error.

In my view, it is the algorithms rather than individual posts that should be the primary target of regulation. Only when platforms are required to stop rewarding outrage will the volume of misinformation fall, and this approach would leave far fewer decisions about truth in the hands of moderators. Education, as the second writer insists, remains essential, but it works best in an environment that is not rigged against it.

2.title: Advertising that crosses the line
2.brief: A national newspaper recently published an article praising a new advertising campaign for an energy drink aimed at teenagers, which uses the slogan 'Sleep is for the weak'. Write a letter to the editor responding to the article, explaining why you consider the campaign irresponsible and what action you believe should be taken.
2.briefEs: Escribe una carta al director de un periódico criticando una campaña publicitaria dirigida a adolescentes y proponiendo medidas.
criteria: Appropriate formal letter conventions and a clear reason for writing.
Fronting and inversion for emphasis (Seldom have I…, So persuasive is the slogan that…).
Reporting verbs with nuance to represent the article fairly (the writer concedes / insinuates / claims).
A controlled shift of register: rhetorical force without losing formality.
2.model:
Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing in response to your article of 14 March, in which the new advertising campaign for an energy drink was described as 'bold, witty and refreshingly honest'. Seldom have I read a piece that so completely overlooked the responsibilities that come with addressing a young audience.

Your correspondent concedes that the slogan 'Sleep is for the weak' is provocative, but insinuates that only humourless adults could object to it. I would suggest that the objection has nothing to do with humour. What concerns me, as a parent and a secondary school teacher, is that the campaign presents sleep deprivation, a well-documented risk to adolescent health, as a badge of strength. So effective is the message that several of my students have already adopted the phrase, usually while explaining why they have not done their homework.

It is worth recalling what the evidence tells us. Teenagers need considerably more sleep than adults, and chronic tiredness has been linked to poor concentration, low mood and an increased likelihood of accidents. A product that combines high levels of caffeine with a message ridiculing rest is not merely tasteless; it actively undermines the efforts of schools and families to promote healthier habits.

Nor is this simply a matter of personal taste. Advertising standards rightly prohibit campaigns that encourage behaviour likely to harm the health of children. I would therefore urge the relevant authority to review the campaign without delay, and I would invite the manufacturer to consider whether a short-term boost in sales is worth the damage to its reputation.

Your article praised the campaign for its honesty. The honest truth, however, is that sleep is not for the weak. It is for anyone who wishes to think clearly, and teenagers deserve to be told so.

Yours faithfully,

Elena Ruiz

3.title: Review: a book about the mind
3.brief: A popular science website is publishing reviews of books that change the way readers think about the mind. Write a review of a book you have read about memory, perception or decision-making. Explain what the book argues, evaluate how convincingly it does so, and say who would benefit most from reading it.
3.briefEs: Escribe una reseña de un libro de divulgación sobre la memoria, la percepción o la toma de decisiones para una web de ciencia.
criteria: Modals of speculation and deduction in present and past (must have, can't have, may well be).
A contrast between needn't have and didn't need to, or a modal perfect of criticism (should have, could have).
Will/would for assumption or characteristic behaviour (Readers will recognise…, She would always…).
Precise cognition vocabulary (discern, perceive, glimpse, bias) and a clear recommendation.
3.model:
The Unreliable Narrator Inside Your Head

Anyone who has ever argued with a sibling about a shared childhood memory will recognise the premise of 'The Editing Room', a lively and occasionally unsettling account of how the brain rewrites the past. Its author, a cognitive psychologist, argues that memory is less an archive than a newsroom, constantly revising its stories to fit what we now believe.

The early chapters are the strongest. Drawing on experiments in which volunteers were persuaded to 'remember' events that never happened, the author shows how readily we fill gaps with plausible detail. Most readers will have assumed that a vivid memory must be an accurate one; by the end of chapter three, they will be far less sure. Particularly memorable is a section on eyewitness testimony, in which she traces how a single leading question can reshape what a witness believes she perceived.

The book is less convincing when it turns to self-help. A chapter promising techniques to 'bias-proof' your decisions feels like an afterthought, and its advice, to slow down and consider alternatives, is sensible but hardly revelatory. The author needn't have included it at all; the science is fascinating enough without the promise of practical benefits. Similarly, she might have acknowledged more openly that some of the studies she cites have not been fully replicated, a caveat a careful reader can only glimpse in the endnotes.

These reservations aside, the writing is clear, witty and refreshingly free of jargon. The author has a gift for the telling example, and she will often pause mid-argument to describe an experiment so vividly that you can almost see the puzzled volunteers.

Who should read it? Students of psychology will find little that is new, but anyone curious about why their memories feel so certain, and are so often wrong, could hardly find a better introduction. It may well change the way you tell your own stories.

3.title: Trusting your gut
3.brief:
Read the two texts below. Write an essay summarising and evaluating the key points from both texts. Use your own words throughout as far as possible, and include your own ideas in your answer.

Text 1 — The wisdom of intuition
Experienced professionals often make excellent decisions in seconds, without being able to explain how. A veteran firefighter senses that a floor is about to collapse; a nurse notices that a patient 'just doesn't look right' hours before the monitors confirm it. Such intuitions are not mystical. They are the product of thousands of hours of pattern recognition, and to dismiss them in favour of slow, explicit analysis is to throw away valuable expertise.

Text 2 — The limits of the gut
Intuition feels reliable precisely because it arrives with a sense of certainty, but that certainty is often misplaced. In fields where feedback is slow or unclear, such as investment or long-term forecasting, experts' instincts perform little better than chance. Worse, gut feelings are shaped by prejudice and recent experience as much as by expertise. Important decisions should be tested against evidence, however confident we feel.
3.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo que resuma y evalúe dos textos sobre la intuición frente al análisis en la toma de decisiones.
criteria: Accurate summaries of both texts in your own words.
Modals of deduction and speculation used to evaluate claims (may well be, cannot always be).
Vocabulary of cognition and bias (perceive, discern, misplaced confidence, cognitive bias).
A balanced conclusion that identifies when each approach is appropriate.
3.model:
Both texts consider how far we should rely on intuition when making decisions, though they place their emphasis very differently.

The first text defends intuition as a form of compressed expertise. Its writer argues that skilled practitioners can discern danger or illness almost instantly because years of experience have trained them to recognise patterns they cannot consciously articulate. To disregard such judgements in favour of laborious analysis, she suggests, would be to waste knowledge that has been hard won. The examples of the firefighter and the nurse are persuasive, and most of us will have encountered professionals whose instincts proved uncannily accurate.

The second text, however, cautions that the confidence intuition brings is not proof of its accuracy. Its author observes that in areas where outcomes emerge slowly, experts' hunches may be barely more reliable than guesses, and that instinct is easily distorted by bias and by whatever happens to be fresh in our minds. Decisions of consequence, he concludes, ought to be checked against evidence.

On reflection, the two positions can be reconciled. Intuition is likely to be trustworthy only where people have had extensive practice and rapid, clear feedback, which is precisely the situation of the firefighter and the nurse. Where feedback is delayed or ambiguous, the gut may well be little more than a confident storyteller. The real skill, then, lies in recognising which kind of situation one is in. A doctor who acts on a hunch in an emergency is behaving sensibly; a minister who stakes a national budget on one cannot be said to be doing the same. Instinct deserves respect, but it should not be allowed to escape scrutiny.

4.title: Report on a graduate mentoring scheme
4.brief: Your organisation introduced a pilot mentoring scheme last year, pairing new graduate employees with senior staff. The director has asked you to write a report evaluating the scheme. Your report should assess what has worked well, identify any problems, and make recommendations about whether and how the scheme should be extended.
4.briefEs: Escribe un informe para la dirección evaluando un programa piloto de mentoría para empleados recién graduados y con recomendaciones.
criteria: Clear report layout with headings and an objective, impersonal tone.
Nominalisation and complex noun phrases (the introduction of, a reduction in staff turnover).
Participle and reduced relative clauses (staff taking part, the problems identified).
Verb patterns with a change of meaning (stopped attending / stopped to reflect; tried to arrange / tried meeting).
4.model:
Introduction
The purpose of this report is to evaluate the graduate mentoring pilot introduced in January and to make recommendations regarding its future. The findings are based on a survey completed by all twenty-four participants and on interviews with six mentors.

Strengths of the scheme
The most significant outcome has been a marked improvement in graduate retention. Of the twelve graduates taking part, eleven remain with the company, compared with an average of seven in previous intakes. Participants consistently attributed their decision to stay to the guidance received from their mentors, particularly in the early months. A number also reported a greater understanding of how decisions are made across departments, something rarely acquired through formal training alone.

Problems identified
The principal difficulty concerned time. Several mentors, faced with heavy workloads, stopped attending scheduled meetings after the first quarter, leaving their mentees uncertain whom to approach. Others tried to arrange sessions outside working hours, which proved unpopular. In addition, the absence of clear objectives meant that some pairings drifted into informal conversations with little lasting value. Mentors who tried setting specific goals at the outset, by contrast, described their sessions as considerably more productive.

Recommendations
In view of these findings, it is recommended that the scheme be extended to all graduate employees from next year, subject to the following changes:
• the allocation of protected time, of at least two hours per month, for mentoring activities;
• the introduction of a brief training session for mentors, covering goal-setting and feedback;
• a mid-year review allowing either party to request a different pairing if the relationship is not working.

Conclusion
Despite the problems outlined above, the pilot has demonstrated clear benefits at relatively low cost. With the adjustments proposed, there is every reason to believe that an extended scheme would make a lasting contribution to the development and retention of new staff.

4.title: Is failure overrated?
4.brief:
Read the two texts below. Write an essay summarising and evaluating the key points from both texts. Use your own words throughout as far as possible, and include your own ideas in your answer.

Text 1 — Fail fast, fail often
The most innovative organisations treat failure not as a disgrace but as information. Every unsuccessful experiment eliminates a possibility and brings the team closer to a solution. Cultures that punish mistakes produce employees who never take risks, and companies that never take risks are eventually overtaken by those that do. Celebrating intelligent failure is therefore not a luxury but a condition of progress.

Text 2 — The cult of the comeback
It has become fashionable to romanticise failure, particularly among those who have already succeeded. The entrepreneur who jokes about his three bankrupt start-ups rarely mentions the family money that cushioned each fall. For most people, failure means debt, anxiety and lost opportunities that never return. Encouraging the young to 'fail often' without acknowledging these costs is not inspiring; it is irresponsible.
4.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo que resuma y evalúe dos textos sobre si se idealiza el fracaso.
criteria: Faithful summaries of both texts without lifting phrases.
Nominalisation for a formal academic style (the celebration of failure, a reluctance to take risks).
Participle clauses to condense information (Having summarised…, Writing from…).
Collocations with make/take/do/have at C2 (take a calculated risk, make allowances for, have a bearing on).
4.model:
Both texts examine the current enthusiasm for failure as a route to success, but they assess its value in sharply contrasting ways.

The first text presents failure as a source of learning. According to its writer, each unsuccessful attempt narrows the range of possibilities and thereby advances the search for a solution. Organisations that penalise error, he argues, discourage risk-taking and will ultimately lose ground to more adventurous competitors. The celebration of well-judged failure is consequently portrayed as essential to innovation. This is a reasonable position, and it has a clear bearing on fields such as research and product design, where experimentation is unavoidable.

The second text, however, questions who can actually afford to fail. Its author suggests that the glorification of failure is largely the work of people whose setbacks were softened by wealth or connections, and that for the majority the consequences are far more serious and lasting. Urging young people to embrace failure without recognising these risks is, in her view, reckless. Writing from the perspective of those without such safety nets, she raises a point that the first text conspicuously ignores.

In my opinion, the two positions are complementary rather than contradictory. The first describes the conditions under which failure can be productive; the second reminds us that those conditions are unevenly distributed. The real challenge, therefore, is not to choose between celebrating and fearing failure, but to extend to more people the security that makes it possible to take a calculated risk. Institutions that genuinely wish to encourage innovation must make allowances for mistakes, but they must also ensure that a single failure does not have ruinous consequences for those who make it.

5.title: AI in the laboratory
5.brief:
Read the two texts below. Write an essay summarising and evaluating the key points from both texts. Use your own words throughout as far as possible, and include your own ideas in your answer.

Text 1 — A new scientific revolution
Artificial intelligence is reported to have predicted the structures of millions of proteins, identified promising antibiotics and detected patterns in astronomical data that human researchers had overlooked for decades. By taking over the most laborious stages of research, AI frees scientists to concentrate on the questions that matter most. Far from threatening science, it is likely to accelerate discovery on a scale not seen since the invention of the microscope.

Text 2 — Answers without understanding
A prediction is not an explanation. When an algorithm identifies a promising compound, it rarely tells us why, and science that cannot explain its own results risks becoming a form of sophisticated guesswork. There is also a danger that research priorities will be shaped by whatever data happens to be available to train the models, rather than by the questions most worth asking.
5.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo que resuma y evalúe dos textos sobre el papel de la inteligencia artificial en la investigación científica.
criteria: Reporting passives and passive infinitives (is said to have, is thought to be, appears to have been).
Hedging and impersonal structures (it would appear, arguably, there is some evidence that).
Academic collocations (draw conclusions, pose a challenge, shed light on).
A reasoned personal view that weighs both texts.
5.model:
The two texts consider the growing role of artificial intelligence in scientific research, the first celebrating its potential and the second questioning what kind of knowledge it produces.

According to the first writer, AI has already achieved remarkable results, from modelling protein structures to uncovering overlooked patterns in data. By automating time-consuming tasks, it is said to allow researchers to focus on the most significant problems, and its impact is compared to that of the microscope. The achievements cited are undeniably impressive, and it would appear that AI can indeed shed light on problems that have resisted conventional methods for years. Nevertheless, the text arguably treats speed of discovery as if it were the only measure of scientific progress.

The second writer addresses precisely this limitation. She argues that predictions generated by algorithms frequently come without any account of the mechanisms behind them, and that a science unable to explain its findings is in danger of becoming educated guesswork. She also warns that the availability of data, rather than the importance of a question, may come to determine what is studied.

In my view, both concerns are legitimate, but they are not incompatible. AI is best regarded as a powerful instrument for generating hypotheses, which must then be tested and explained by human researchers. There is some evidence that this is already happening in many laboratories, where algorithmic predictions are treated as starting points rather than conclusions. The greater challenge, I would suggest, is institutional: funding bodies must continue to support questions that do not lend themselves to data-driven approaches. If they do so, AI need not undermine scientific understanding; it may well deepen it.

5.title: Privacy is not dead
5.brief: A technology magazine is running a series of articles titled 'Is privacy dead?'. Write an article responding to the question. You should consider how much personal data people now give away, why it matters, and what individuals and governments can realistically do to protect privacy.
5.briefEs: Escribe un artículo para una revista de tecnología respondiendo a la pregunta '¿Ha muerto la privacidad?'.
criteria: An engaging title and a lively but controlled semi-formal register.
Causatives (have your data analysed, get your settings changed, have someone check).
Reporting passives (is estimated to, is believed to have been).
Hedging language to avoid overstatement (arguably, it seems, to a large extent).
5.model:
Privacy Isn't Dead. It's Just Badly Neglected.

This morning, before I had finished my first coffee, I had my location tracked by three apps, my heart rate logged by a watch and my reading habits analysed by a news site I barely remember signing up for. None of this was dramatic. None of it required a hacker in a dark room. And that, arguably, is the problem: privacy is not being stolen from us so much as quietly given away.

The scale of that giveaway is hard to grasp. The average smartphone is estimated to share data with dozens of companies every day, most of which its owner has never heard of. Much of this information seems harmless in isolation. Combined, however, it can reveal where we live, whom we love, what we fear and how much we might be willing to pay. Several large databases are believed to have been sold on or leaked in recent years, often without the people concerned ever finding out.

Why should we care if we have nothing to hide? Because privacy is not about hiding; it is about control. It allows us to decide who knows what about us, and to change our minds. Without it, we become, to a large extent, predictable, and therefore easier to manipulate.

So what can be done? Individually, quite a lot more than most of us bother to do. It takes ten minutes to get your app permissions reviewed, and many phones will now have unnecessary tracking switched off at a single tap. But individual effort has limits. Governments must require that privacy be the default setting rather than an option buried in the menus, and they must have companies' data practices audited by regulators with real powers.

Privacy, then, is not dead. It is simply in poor health, and like most patients, it will recover only if somebody takes it seriously.
